Okay, so my boyfriend (who doesn't voat) is a gun guy. He recently acquired a Billings (Billings & Spencer) breech loading shotgun. It is missing the barrel and all of the ejector parts. The more we look for information on this gun, the more confusing it gets. There is a stamp on the top of the breech that says "C.E.Billings 11/02/1875 patent". He is looking for a blow-up diagram of the gun to see exactly what the missing pieces look like so he can find/fabricate the pieces. It is starting to look like a hopeless search. We've found a plethora of things that Billings patented and built and sold, but not so much on the particular gun sitting beside me on the sofa. Can anybody help? I can post pictures if you want to see. :)
There were only around 300 patents issued on 11/02/1875, have you just looked through all the ones issued that day? I'm going to go ahead and do that and see if it's in there.

Additionally, the reason it can be so difficult to find records from prior to 1900 or so is that patents were almost all limited to drawings so they're difficult to digitize beyond scanning them in. There's an intern or three at the patent office who just scan in the old records all day as they are able; almost no one goes looking for historical patents like this so you have to know how to deal with their system to actually find shit, and sometimes that's just looking at every patent issued for a given day. These patents also don't have any of the searchable metadata attached to them such as the name of the applicant, company, and so on, so it's very much like having to go to the actual office and search through physical records.

Is this it? H. C. Bull, "Breech Loading Fire-Arm," Patent No. 169,413 issued on 11/02/1875. Link to Patent.

EDIT: Nope. Patent 280 out of 298 results for that day is C. E. Billings, "Breech-Loading Fire-Arm", Patent No. 169,335. Link to Patent.
You are my hero!!! how did you find that? I had a friend who is a patent attorney looking and he couldn't find it!

It's because patent attorneys don't have to look very far back. I'm a historical archaeologist so I'm used to combing through document databases like this. Like I was saying in another comment, these documents are normally scanned by unpaid interns and given just enough searchable metadata to categorize them properly (in this case the date) and nothing else because it just takes way too much time to read the entire document and fill out all the fields like names. So I pulled every patent that was issued on 11/02/1875 - 298 of them - and then looked at each one. As luck would have it, the Billings Breech-Loader was near the end so I had to go through basically all of them. It ended up taking about an hour or an hour and a half of actual attention but it wasn't too bad.
